articles.title: Able2Shell: Frequently asked questions for reported N-able N-central zero-day vulnerabilities
articles.context: As of November 10, there are no details available for any threat actor activity connected to Able2Shell exploitation
articles.full_text:
N-able released a hotfix for N-central that fixes seven CVEs after a researcher published proof-of-concept code for 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities. The researcher says one attack chain needs no credentials.

Key Takeaways

Able2Shell is a set of 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-able N-central, published with proof-of-concept code. The researcher says one chain lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server.

Security firms report exploitation attempts against N-central honeypots, but as of November 10, no confirmed compromise of a customer server has been reported.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 on November 10. It fixes seven CVEs.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Able2Shell, a set of reported zero-day vulnerabilities in N-able N-central.

FAQ

When was Able2Shell first disclosed?

A researcher operating under the GitHub account “Oracle-Security” published a write-up titled “Able2Shell” in the account’s CVEs repository. It describes 33 alleged N-central vulnerabilities with proof-of-concept code. The earliest README commit is dated November 9, 2026 at 04:14 UTC. N-able described the release as a public disclosure by an independent security researcher. N-able does not state whether it was notified in advance and does not name the researcher.

What are the vulnerabilities associated with Able2Shell?

On November 10, N-able published seven CVE records for vulnerabilities fixed in N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2. On its status page, N-able says the release addresses “the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities” and that a follow-up hotfix will provide further security updates. The page lists all seven as related CVEs. One, CVE-2026-91000, had been reserved on September 14, before the public Able2Shell disclosure.

N-able’s CVE titles match several finding types in the researcher’s README, but N-able has not said which of the 33 findings each CVE addresses. N-able credits CVE-2026-125882 to Nate Fair of Sprocket Security, and a file repository path traversal also appears in the README.

Is Able2Shell one vulnerability or several?

Several. The README lists 33 findings, and some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list. The researcher lists four exploit chains. The rest are standalone findings.

The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required. The researcher’s proof-of-concept takes several identifiers as inputs, and other findings in the README describe anonymous ways to obtain some of them. The XXE step has the appliance fetch a file from an attacker-hosted server.For the MMS3 chains, the researcher says an unauthenticated attacker can plant the script, which runs when a logged-in administrator views the poisoned patch details. N-able’s record for CVE-2026-125880 lists high privileges and active user interaction.

How severe is Able2Shell?

Two of the four chains reach root: MMS3 stored XSS to Audit Export, and SIS path traversal to syslog. The XXE chain runs commands as the nable account (uid 992), and the researcher’s proof-of-concept can also create an administrator account. N-able’s CVSSv4 scores for the seven CVEs range from 8.3 to 9.3, and N-able calls Hotfix 2 a critical security update.

Has N-able confirmed the findings?

N-able has published seven CVEs and a hotfix, but it has not mapped its CVEs to the researcher’s 33 findings or commented on them individually. Before the hotfix, N-able said it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in N-central by an independent security researcher.

Which versions are affected?

N-able's CVE records list N-central versions before 26.4.1 as affected (the record for CVE-2026-91000 writes this as 2026.4.1), and the fixed build is 2026.4.1.26. The researcher says all testing was done on N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, which the researcher describes as a pre-release build, and that "most if not all vulnerabilities should work on previous versions."

Is the hosted N-central service affected?

N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline as a precaution after the disclosure, and its status page lists hosted N-central in the Americas, APAC and Europe among the affected services. On November 10, N-able said all hosted N-central servers across all global regions had been upgraded to the new release. Hosted customers still upgrade their own Agents and Probes.

Has Able2Shell been exploited in the wild?

N-able's status page says it is observing “scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code.” Huntress reported N-able’s statement that it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited, and said on November 10 that it had not observed evidence of Able2Shell exploitation in its partners’ environments.

Beazley Security Labs updated its November 9 advisory on November 10 with watchTowr’s report of exploitation attempts against its N-central honeypots. Beazley Security Labs says a confirmed compromise of a customer server “has not been reported.”

Previdian reports exploitation attempts against its N-central decoy environment, not confirmed compromise. Its decoys recorded 68 events from one source IP address starting on November 9, including XXE and sensitive-file access attempts. Previdian says these do not show a completed account takeover or command execution, or a full replay of the published chain.

Which threat actors are exploiting Able2Shell?

As of November 10, there are no details available for any threat actor activity connected to Able2Shell exploitation.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. The researcher’s README includes Python proof-of-concept code for the alleged vulnerabilities, tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31.

How does this relate to earlier N-central vulnerabilities?

Able2Shell is a newly disclosed set of vulnerabilities, and it is not known whether any relate to earlier N-central flaws. None of the seven CVEs fixed in Hotfix 2 is in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog as of November 10. Five earlier N-central CVEs are in the KEV catalog:

CVE

Description

Authentication bypass

CVE-2025-8876

CVE-2025-8875

August 13, 2025

Are patches or mitigations available?

Yes. On November 10, N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), which fixes the seven CVEs above. According to N-able, on-premises customers upgrade their own servers, while N-able upgrades hosted servers. All customers also upgrade their Agents and Probes, Agents first, because an upgraded Probe cannot communicate with Agents that have not been upgraded. Until an on-premises server is upgraded, N-able recommends keeping it offline. A follow-up hotfix with further security updates is also planned. Hotfix 2 removes legacy mobile device management (MDM). The release notes list N-central’s built-in remote control as temporarily disabled, while Take Control continues to work.Are there indicators of compromise?

Yes. Beazley Security Labs and Previdian have published network indicators tied to exploitation attempts, including source IP addresses and the SOAP endpoints targeted. Huntress recommends reviewing login and authentication activity from November 8 onward, and watching for anomalous remote access sessions, newly deployed scripts and unauthorized new administrator accounts.

Has Tenable released product coverage?

A list of Tenable plugins for these vulnerabilities can be found on the individual CVE pages:

This list may contain plugins released after this blog’s publication.

Has Tenable classified any of these vulnerabilities under Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. Tenable has classified CVE-2026-125883 as a Vulnerability of Interest (VOI) under Vulnerability Watch. CVE-2026-125878, CVE-2026-125881 and CVE-2026-125882 are each classified as a Vulnerability Being Monitored (VBM).

Elevation of Privilege (EoP) vulnerabilities accounted for 48.9% of the vulnerabilities patched this month, followed by remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities at 27.1%.

Moderate

CVE-2026-124194 | Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 is a spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. It received a CVSSv3 score of 6.5 and is rated moderate. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a target to open a crafted Microsoft Office file. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to obtain the target’s valid NTLMv2 hash, which can then be used to impersonate that user in follow-on attacks.

According to Microsoft, this vulnerability was exploited in the wild as a zero-day. Additionally, the advisory credits this discovery to a security researcher that used Claude, the large language model (LLM) from Anthropic, though no specific version of Claude was noted in the advisory.

Critical

CVE-2026-118146 | Windows Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118146 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Active Directory Domain Services. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Active Directory Domain Services to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Important

CVE-2026-120002 | Microsoft SharePoint Server elevation of privilege vulnerability

CVE-2026-120002 is an EoP vulnerability affecting Microsoft SharePoint Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 9.9 and is rated as important. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Microsoft Office SharePoint to elevate privileges over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to gain elevated privileges. It was assessed as “Exploitation Less Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-118207 | Microsoft Exchange Server remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118207 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could send malformed input to Microsoft Exchange Server, causing code to execute over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-119952 | Windows Schannel remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-119952 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Schannel. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.1 and is rated as critical. An unauthenticated attacker could exploit an observable timing discrepancy in Windows Schannel to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

articles.title: U.S. urges critical infrastructure orgs to secure refrigeration systems ASAP after EU supermarket and blood bank attacks
articles.context: Visualize attack paths and prevent lateral movement: Threat actors frequently exploit web-exposed IT infrastructure to pivot laterally into critical OT environments
articles.full_text:
Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation.

Key takeaways

Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally.

Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food.

CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices.

Critical infrastructure organizations in the healthcare, chemicals, transportation, and food and agriculture sectors must urgently harden their industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems to protect food, medicines, and other essential products against ongoing cyber attacks.

That’s the call from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other U.S. government agencies, following a series of alarming breaches against refrigeration systems in French blood banks and European supermarkets.

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera said in a statement.

Attackers are remotely targeting electronic-temperature and commercial-refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. They’re looking for unpatched vulnerabilities and other security flaws, such as misconfigurations, according to the agencies.

Once attackers gain remote access to these systems, they try to tamper with these machines’ temperature controls to damage their refrigerated products. The temperature changes could also trigger fire hazards.

In a joint fact sheet, the agencies recommend organizations immediately take the following steps:

Use strong authentication mechanisms and change systems’ default passwords.

Keep systems updated and promptly patch critical vulnerabilities.

Replace legacy devices that have reached end-of-life status.

Identify systems accessible from the internet.

Isolate operational technology (OT) systems from business networks.

Remove unnecessary remote access.

Secure necessary remote access.

Maintain offsite backups.

“This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations,” said Brett Leatherman, cyber branch operations director at the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), one of the authoring agencies.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT) also contributed to the joint fact sheet.

Attackers hit hundreds of grocery stores in France several weeks ago that caused food to spoil and triggered fires. The National Cybersecurity Agency of France (ANSSI) recently told Cybersecurity Dive it has been investigating the attacks since they started in mid-October and is aware of compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB controllers.

How Tenable can help defend against recent cold-chain cyber attacks

Recent attacks on cold-chain infrastructure and other types of critical supply-chain infrastructure highlight the importance of asset visibility for security teams. As operational environments become increasingly connected, the line between IT and OT continues to blur, often leaving critical cyber-physical systems inadvertently exposed to the internet.

The Tenable One Exposure Management Platform provides comprehensive visibility and actionable intelligence to heed CISA’s warnings and secure converged IT/OT environments. By unifying cyber exposure signals and threat intelligence across your attack surface, Tenable One helps security teams to seamlessly find, prioritize, and secure vulnerable systems before attackers manipulate them.

Here are some of the ways Tenable supports security teams across industries in mitigating threats, including AI-assisted attacks, to critical OT systems and supply chain infrastructure:

Identify web-exposed assets with attack surface management (ASM): Attackers are actively scanning the web for internet-accessible refrigeration controllers. Tenable One’s external attack surface management (EASM) capabilities allow you to view your infrastructure from an attacker's perspective. By continuously discovering external-facing assets and rogue internet connections, your teams can immediately identify systems accessible from the internet — one of CISA's key directives — and lock down unnecessary remote access points.

Achieve ground-truth OT/CPS visibility: To address critical vulnerabilities and identify end-of-life equipment, you need a complete and accurate asset inventory. Tenable’s purpose-built OT security capabilities deliver a comprehensive inventory of all OT, IoT, and IT assets. By querying deep device details, including the specific firmware version of controllers like the targeted Danfoss and Copeland models, as well as associated known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, Tenable helps eliminate operational blind spots.

Visualize attack paths and prevent lateral movement: Threat actors frequently exploit web-exposed IT infrastructure to pivot laterally into critical OT environments. Tenable One maps critical risks and continuously visualizes viable attack paths, showing exactly how attackers could move through your converged IT and OT environment. These insights enable security teams to effectively enforce network segmentation, block malicious communications, and securely isolate OT systems from business networks.

Prioritize real-world risk and human safety: With a surge of alerts and limited patching windows, security teams need to know what to fix first. Tenable One correlates vulnerability data with threat intelligence, exploitability, deployed compensating controls, and asset context. This context helps your teams focus remediation on critical exposure findings such as default passwords, remote code execution (RCE), or changes in a device’s running state that pose significant and verifiable risk to production uptime and physical safety.

By taking command of your entire attack surface with a unified exposure management strategy, your organization can proactively defend your most critical industrial systems from the evolving global threat of cyber sabotage.

articles.title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
articles.context: What can we learn from this Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk...
articles.full_text:
php2shell raised fears of mass exploitation. A week of testing by our research team found that working exploits had to be fitted to each target’s exact PHP setup. Systems that share one build, such as network appliances, are the exception: one tuned exploit can reach every device that runs it.

Key takeaways

The five vulnerable PHP sites we exposed to the internet were not compromised, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) that go beyond version checks do not reliably confirm whether a host is vulnerable. Exploitation has been confirmed elsewhere, on researcher honeypots and on some network appliances.

In realistic environments, turning php2shell into remote code execution usually takes an exploit built for the specific target. That is hard, not impossible, and it puts php2shell in a different category from Log4Shell, even though both received near-maximum severity ratings. Where many systems share one build, such as network appliances, a single calibrated exploit can work against all of them.

Patch now, starting with internet-facing management interfaces, network appliances, and end-of-life PHP branches. Tenable Nessus and Tenable One Web App Scanning have had version-based detection since October 21.

Background

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced two vulnerabilities, and on October 21 released fixes for flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Each has a CVSSv4 score of 9.2. For a full breakdown of affected versions, fixes and mitigations, see our frequently asked questions blog post.

This post covers what happened after the disclosure, based on what our team observed directly.

From disclosure to headline in under 48 hours

php2shell got big fast. Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online before the official release. Within two days, the vulnerability had a name, a logo and coverage in mainstream media.

Several websites went offline as a precaution, as described in our threat actor response blog post. Censys’s php2shell dashboard, which tracks PHP services by reported version, showed about 30.3 million PHP services still on an affected version on October 29, though a matching version does not mean a system can be exploited.

The comparison with Log4Shell came up early, but the two are very different to exploit. With Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), attackers only had to send a short piece of text to a vulnerable application, for example in a login form or a web request. If the application logged that text, the attack worked. The same text worked against almost any vulnerable target without changes, so attackers could launch it at scale within hours, and many of those attacks succeeded.

php2shell is different. Exploitation depends on the state of the heap, the process manager in use, worker reuse and how memory is laid out on a given build. php2shell drew attention quickly, but attackers can't exploit it as easily as Log4Shell.

What changed while we were testing

Several developments that matter for defenders came after our research began:

On October 24, honeypots run by Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three sensors running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, a configuration that favors the exploit.

On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Federal civilian agencies have until October 29 to remediate.

The same day, security firm Dream reported an attack chain that combined php2shell with a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw, Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300). Dream says the campaign rooted “25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.” Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 says it independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results. We have not verified these findings ourselves.

On October 28, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV catalog and noted that it can be chained with php2shell to run commands as root. By October 29, Palo Alto Networks reported active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.

These reports are consistent with what we found. The exploit has to be calibrated to a specific build. Network appliances often run the same software across many devices, so one calibrated exploit can reach many of them. That is where we expect targeted exploitation to keep growing.

What we observed during our exploit research

Exposed targets

To measure real-world activity, we kept five vulnerable PHP sites reachable from the internet: four through the evening of October 24, and one still running in a standard, vulnerable configuration at the time of writing.

Over that period, we observed mass exploitation attempts that matched php2shell exploitation patterns. None of our targets had been compromised as of October 29.

Other organizations have reported exploitation attempts and, in the cases described above, successful exploitation. Amazon Threat Intelligence says php2shell is “now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.” Our data does not contradict these reports. It shows that attempts, even at scale, were not enough to compromise a default installation in our environment. Attempts and successful compromises are two different numbers, and in the first days after a disclosure people often treat them as the same.

Public proofs-of-concept

We collected and tested almost all public PoCs. An early lead was php2shell poc, published by researcher Daniel Púa (devploit). It let us reproduce the exposure on multiple 8.4 and 8.5 environments with specific configurations. From there, we did deeper research, including white-box testing and code and patch comparison, and achieved remote code execution on PHP 7.4.33.

What we learned from this research is that the exploit inadvertently reveals a clean discriminator: the same multipart POST that begins stage 1 produces a different allocator response on patched vs. unpatched PHP. No heap corruption, no crash, no shell, just a measurable size difference in how the server handles the request. That became signal 1: a large filename in the multipart request produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable versions than on fixed versions, because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Same request, same PHP – different memory behavior depending solely on whether the UAF patch is present.

Tenable Research identified a second signal as well: the compact amplification sequences that exercise the UAF window's existence without triggering corruption. The session upload-progress oracle watches for the crash/recover pattern that vulnerable versions exhibit under controlled amplification.

These two signals became a stateful probe that a Nessus ‘direct check’ plugin could detect. However, the probe would miss some vulnerable systems and flag some patched ones as vulnerable.

The memory corruption is real, and PHP confirms memory disclosure as one of the impacts. Turning it into code execution on a target is difficult and unique to each target. Our working RCE required an exploit tuned to the target's environment, including its PHP build, SAPI, extensions and runtime configuration. A payload that works against one lab setup does not carry over to a different distribution package or a different PHP-FPM pool configuration.

AI-accelerated research: Useful, but it needs checking

AI agents sped up our reverse engineering and testing, and they also produced at least one convincing false positive. During a multi-hour session, an agent built a working shell against our PHP-FPM lab containers and reported it as confirmation of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. It was not. The agent had used a local file inclusion weakness that we had added to the lab, a different attack class that does not exist in default PHP deployments. A researcher caught the error by checking the exploit chain against the vulnerability's mechanics.

The lesson applies to anyone reading exploitation claims this week: a real shell is not proof that a specific CVE was used. We also ran into inconsistent responses from AI tools when doing authorized exploit validation, which slowed parts of the work.

White-box testing

The GDB analysis and heap geometry research below show why: there is no universal offset. Code execution is a real exposure yet it is not as simple as portrayed. The RCE we achieved on PHP 7.4.33 worked only once the exploit matched that one setup. A profile that achieves a shell against one lab container does not carry over to a different distribution package, a different PHP-FPM pool configuration, or a different memory limit.

The chunk-relative offsets pictured in the ‘heap geometry capture method’ visuals below reference _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0, arData at chunk+0x64b80. These values illustrate the measurement method and are specific to PHP 8.3.35 built from the docker-library bookworm image on amd64. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or a PHP 8.3.35 built with different extensions, produces different chunk geometry values. We used GDB against the live worker to measure the actual values for a given target.

Our failure to show that mass exploitation is quick or easy does not make this vulnerability harmless. A well-resourced attacker who wants a specific target can build that exploit, and AI-assisted tooling shortens the time it takes. It does make mass exploitation of the Log4Shell kind much less likely. The exception is any population of systems that share one build, such as network appliances, where the cost of calibration is paid once.

Why exploitation is hard

When possible, Tenable Research releases exposure direct checks to help customers detect exploitable vulnerabilities within their environments. These direct checks depend on finding reliable and safe methods of exercising a vulnerability in a way that simulates an exploit without triggering any destructive actions. This typically involves first researching how to develop an exploit, then figuring out how to test that safely.

Our research found the php2shell exposure difficult to reproduce broadly, even with white-box testing and GDB attached to processes, and even with AI agents analyzing runtime memory and source code for weaknesses and leads in parallel. What we learned from this research helps to inform us on the practical realities of real-world exploitation:

php2shell is a multi-stage memory corruption chain. A direct check triggering an out-of-memory condition alone does not fully guarantee the asset is also exposed to remote code execution.

In-memory offsets are version and system specific. The chunk-relative structure offsets required for heap manipulation change with every PHP patch release and system/software combination. Gaps in an inventory of known offsets and platforms could make a vulnerable system look patched (false-negative).

The OOM trigger depends on application-controlled memory limits. Whether the condition fires depends on the configured memory_limit and on whether the application overrides it via ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives.

The use-after-free requires reuse of the PHP worker across consecutive requests. Under mod_php, keep-alive pins a connection to one worker; under FPM, session affinity (PHPSESSID) is required. Both depend on SAPI and process-manager settings. For example, pm.max_requests recycles workers and breaks the use-after-free chain with no visible sign, so the check returns a false negative.

The exploit crashes PHP workers. Workers appear to respawn reliably, but a direct check that intentionally degrades performance could still affect production systems.

What can we learn from this

Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk reaction is triggered that creates significant fears of mass exploitation and extreme risk. While we do not want to downplay the dangers of this vulnerability, it is valuable to understand the practicalities of exploitation in the real world versus the fear that is built around a CVE during the regular news cycle. In this case, that nuance points remediation first at internet-facing assets, especially appliances such as network infrastructure management interfaces, and anything else that runs a common, basic deployment that reduces overall complexity.

Prioritization matters more as AI finds more vulnerabilities

Calif, OpenAI and Wiz are credited with finding php2shell. Calif says AI assisted the discovery. We expect the number of disclosed vulnerabilities to keep rising as these tools improve, and many of them will come with high base scores. Patching everything rated critical at the speed of the news cycle will not be possible.

Security teams need to understand what a vulnerability takes to exploit, not only how bad the worst case is:

Is there a public exploit that works without changes, or only a crash PoC?

Does exploitation depend on a non-default configuration, a specific build or prior access?

Is the vulnerable component reachable from the internet in your environment?

Has anyone observed successful compromise, as opposed to scanning?

Exploit prediction scores such as EPSS, Tenable's Vulnerability Priority Rating (VPR) and confirmed exploitation sources such as CISA's KEV catalog help answer these questions. They work better alongside an analysis of the vulnerability itself than in place of one.

Patch anyway

Our observations do not mean php2shell should be ignored. The conditions for exploitation exist, exploit development will improve and targeted attacks against high-value PHP applications are plausible. Updating to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or applying your distribution's fixed packages, remains the recommendation. For end-of-life branches, plan an upgrade. Until then, apply the configuration mitigations described in our FAQ and limit internet exposure, starting with appliance management interfaces. For network appliances, PHP version numbers do not apply: use your vendor's fixed build or its interim mitigations.

What we are recommending is a different order of work. Patch or isolate internet-facing network appliances, management interfaces, and end-of-life PHP systems now. For the rest of your PHP estate, patch on your critical schedule, and check that less publicized vulnerabilities that are easy to exploit in your environment are not waiting behind php2shell.

articles.title: Whole-of-state defense: How SLED agencies can secure critical infrastructure in the AI era
articles.context: The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure,...
articles.full_text:
AI is widening the attack surface of the critical infrastructure facilities and services that state, local, and education (SLED) organizations run. In the final post of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we explain how a whole-of-state security approach can help SLED agencies protect their critical infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Because cyber attackers prey on under-resourced targets, they often go after SLED organizations, especially those that operate critical infrastructure, including water systems, hospitals, mass transit, emergency services, and schools.

In the latest research from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO), nearly 90% of state CIOs rated cyberattacks on critical systems as a high concern.

AI expands the attack surface in two fundamental ways: SLED agencies and employees adopt AI tools and AI-built apps faster than security teams can authorize and inventory them, while attackers use AI automation to find weak points faster.

A whole-of-state cybersecurity approach treats state agencies, counties, cities, school districts, and utilities as one defensive perimeter, with shared visibility, shared services, and clear governance.

Cyber attackers often look for the weakest link that can offer them an entry point into larger targets. If they can’t crack a state agency’s hardened systems, they’ll try to breach it in a roundabout way by first breaking into a small town’s water utility, a rural school district, or a county dispatch center, and then attempt to move laterally toward the bigger target.

When one of those weak links fails, the consequences can reach well beyond the breached agency: halted 911 dispatches, disrupted water service, exposed resident data, and more.

AI is further complicating the picture.

State, local, and education (SLED) organizations are adopting AI quickly to improve efficiency, employees are building applications with it informally, and adversaries are using it to speed up reconnaissance. Each of those developments is making it harder for security teams to protect SLED agencies.

In this fourth and final blog in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we focus on what that expanding AI attack surface means for state, local, and education cybersecurity leaders responsible for critical infrastructure, and how whole-of-state cybersecurity can help them stay ahead.

Why SLED critical infrastructure is a prime target

SLED organizations operate critical infrastructure, such as water treatment plants, transportation systems, public hospitals, schools, and emergency communications, across many of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors categorized by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

State technology leaders are concerned about protecting these critical infrastructure facilities and services from cyber attacks, as “The Expanding Cyber Perimeter” report, published in September by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO) and General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), found.

Here are five key findings from the report, which drew on the 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey, the 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte Cybersecurity Study, and interviews with state CISOs:

Nearly 90% of state CIOs rate cyber attacks on critical systems as a high concern. The rest rate them as moderate.

State CIOs report low confidence in local governments’ cyber practices. The report’s authors also say it’s unclear how states should help local governments and independent local government entities, like special districts.

Water and wastewater plants, dams, hospitals, and transportation services face the greatest cyber risk.

Many systems run on aging or proprietary operational technology (OT) with no upgrade path, and broad remote access increases their cyber risk.

Small communities and special districts often have limited cyber staff, aging equipment, and complex OT with few controls. With hundreds of such entities in a single state, attackers have plenty of entry points to try.

Responsibility is also murky. According to the NASCIO-GDIT report, it’s often unclear which agency is responsible for responding to an attack on critical infrastructure, especially where legal authority, governance, or partnerships aren’t in place.

Cyber risk extends beyond technical and geographical boundaries. When an attacker breaches systems of a county water utility or a school district, the incident can have widespread consequences.

State and local officials and their CIOs and CISOs should stop treating these incidents as one city’s or one county’s problem. Robert Beach, then CTO of the City of Cocoa, Florida, and a member of the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) executive committee, told StateScoop last year that an attack on critical infrastructure “is an attack on the nation.”

Insiders add another layer of risk. Another MS-ISAC report, “Strengthening Critical Infrastructure: SLTT Progress & Priorities,” published in August 2025, flagged excessive access to system controls as a vulnerability. The report recommended agencies review who can reach their networks and disable credentials promptly when employees leave.

The 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte study underscores the risk, noting that attackers exploit compromised credentials and former employee accounts, so regular access reviews and prompt offboarding remain essential.

Recent cyber attacks against water systems have made the threat very real. On July 30, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) warned that water and wastewater sector utilities in at least seven states had reported cyber attacks, leading in some cases to degraded water operations.

That same day, the CISA said it had observed “a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers” in the water and wastewater sector.

“Threat actors targeting exposed PLCs have modified passwords to lock out operators and disconnected the PLCs by changing their IP addresses. This activity has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” the CISA alert reads.

A week earlier, CISA and several federal agencies had published a joint advisory warning critical infrastructure organizations in the government, water, and energy sectors of “ongoing cyber exploitation of internet-connected OT devices.”

Tenable researchers recommend removing internet-exposed PLCs and setting their mode switches to “Run”, among other steps. The U.S. government is also tightening cybersecurity regulations for water and wastewater utilities.

Federal and state leaders are mobilizing, too.

In August, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, and Texas Cyber Command Chief Vice Admiral (Ret.) TJ White launched Project Watershed at a roundtable in San Antonio, Texas, which I was honored to attend. Project Watershed is a joint effort aimed at strengthening the cybersecurity of Texas water and wastewater systems against threats from hostile foreign adversaries.

Governor Abbott said that through the project, “our communities and water systems will be better secured from the onslaught of cyber-attacks.”

Protecting the water systems Americans rely on every day is a shared responsibility, and Project Watershed shows the kind of public-private collaboration a whole-of-state approach depends on.

How AI expands the attack surface

AI has moved from pilot project to operational reality in state government. NASCIO’s 2026 research shows AI overtaking cybersecurity as the top policy priority for state CIOs, the first time in more than a decade that cybersecurity loses the top spot.

AI adoption is good news for service delivery, but it also increases SLED agencies’ cyber risk. Three forces drive the rise in cyber risk:

Employees build and adopt AI tools on their own. As we covered earlier in this series, non-technical staff can now use AI tools to generate working applications using natural-language prompts, often without permission from the IT and security departments. In a government setting, those unsanctioned apps can access resident data, case management systems, and internal credentials, all without testing, patching, or monitoring.

AI shows up inside the software SLED agencies already own, as vendors quietly add AI features and connectors to their products, which can expand data access and permissions without the awareness of the IT and security teams.

Attackers use automation to move faster. The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure, as the window between when an exposure appears and when attackers exploit it keeps shrinking.

For critical infrastructure operators, the stakes rise further. Their aging OT systems with broad remote access are already a soft target. Unvetted AI apps, over-permissioned connectors, and automated scanning by attackers quickly multiply the number of paths an attacker can chain together.

The key for SLED agency CISOs is to see their exposures across IT, OT, cloud, identity, and AI as one connected picture, and to prioritize and act on the ones an attacker could realistically exploit to reach systems that matter to public safety. An exposure management program can help SLED agencies address this cyber risk with comprehensive visibility, prioritization, and AI-assisted action.

What a whole-of-state approach looks like

A whole-of-state approach treats state agencies, local governments, schools, and utilities as one defensive perimeter instead of a collection of individual, siloed organizations.

The state government should share governance frameworks, visibility of IT/OT assets and security findings, and cybersecurity capabilities so the smallest entity doesn’t have to defend itself alone.

As Tenable’s Matt Kucik explains in the blog, “Whole-of-state cybersecurity: Uniting SLED agencies for maximum impact,” success starts with leadership and vision, open communication, and an actionable plan.

The model is gaining ground. The NASCIO-GDIT report found that 73% of states responding to the 2026 State CIO Survey include critical infrastructure cyber protection in their whole-of-state plans. It calls these models the main framework emerging for statewide resilience. Maturity varies widely, though. Four building blocks separate strong programs from weak ones:

Governance and clear roles. CISA’s state cybersecurity governance case studies highlight Georgia and Virginia, which use formal structures to treat cyber risk as a collective priority. They have proactively defined who is in charge of prevention, who is in charge of responding, and who is in charge of generating incident reports.

Shared visibility. You can’t prioritize what you can’t see. A statewide view of assets and exposures lets a small water district benefit from the same insight as a large state agency.

Shared services. In Utah, its federally funded shared services program offers endpoint protection, patching, training, and incident response to roughly 80% of local government entities in the state. The state secured an additional $1.5 million for water-sector cybersecurity.

Trust earned through results. What local partners need from the state is faster remediation, lower costs, and fewer surprises. New Jersey CISO Michael Geraghty made this point in the NASCIO-GDIT report: Telling local governments you’re from the state and here to help doesn’t earn their trust. Results do.

It’s also key to share information quickly. Terry Loftus, CIO of the San Diego County Office of Education and an MS-ISAC committee member, told StateScoop that many districts learn of attacks when they receive a ransomware demand.

State cybersecurity agencies should build channels that proactively push threat intelligence and exposure data to every entity in their state, to increase the chances of preventing attacks.

Five steps SLED agencies can take to boost their cyber defenses

Here’s Tenable’s advice on where to start, whether you lead a state agency, a county IT shop, a school district, or a municipal utility:

Create and continuously update a complete inventory of your critical infrastructure assets, including OT systems, remote access paths, and AI tools and apps. Start with the systems that affect public health and safety.

Prioritize by exploitability and impact. Don’t chase every finding. Focus on the exposures an attacker could realistically chain together to reach water, power, health, or emergency systems. Removing internet-exposed controllers and securing any remote access paths to them should be the highest priority.

Share visibility across jurisdictions. Give small entities access to the same insight larger agencies have, whether through statewide tooling, shared services, or regular information-sharing forums.

Govern AI use before it sprawls. Set clear policies, approved-tool lists, and training for employees who build with AI.

Check if State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP) funding is still available in your state to help fund these priorities.

How Tenable can help SLED agencies

Tenable One gives security teams unified visibility, insights and action across their organizations’ attack surface, including IT, cloud, identity, AI, and OT.

Tenable One OT Exposure capabilities extend that visibility, insight, and action to the OT and extended internet of things (xIoT) devices used by many critical infrastructure organizations.

With Tenable One, SLED teams can see what they have, understand which exposures matter most, and take prioritized actions, maximizing staff and grant dollars to drive down cyber risk.

The City of Raleigh in North Carolina, for example, uses Tenable to ensure the safety and sustainability of its public water systems. To see how Tenable supports statewide programs, explore our state, local, and education solutions and learn how Tenable helps meet SLCGP requirements.

Looking ahead

The attack surface is growing, a trend that AI is accelerating. Federal funding is shrinking, and its future is uncertain. Yet the fundamentals of resilience stay the same: know your assets, understand your exposures, share what you learn, and act together before an attacker forces your hand.

No single state or jurisdiction has solved this, and no single tool will. A whole-of-state approach gives SLED organizations the best chance to stay ahead of the threats facing the critical services residents rely on every day.

Learn how Tenable helps SLED organizations implement statewide exposure management and align with SLCGP requirements.

articles.full_text:
Researchers have demonstrated remote code execution through CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) are available. Software that uses the decoder includes Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients and PHP for Windows.

Change log

Update October 28: Added a section on how reliable exploitation of CVE-2026-111497 has been so far, based on research from ELLIO and Imperva.

Click here to review the change log history

Update October 28: Added a section on how reliable exploitation of CVE-2026-111497 has been so far, based on research from ELLIO and Imperva.

Update October 27: CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog.

October 26: Original publication.

Key Takeaways

CVE-2026-111497, known as Brotli2Shell and by several other names, is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library that Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), scored 9.2 under CVSSv4.0.

Any application that decompresses attacker-controlled data with a vulnerable Brotli decoder is potentially at risk, including Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients, FFmpeg, Apache Arrow and ClickHouse.

Patches are available for Google Brotli and the major runtimes, though some projects had not shipped a fixed release as of October 26, and applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli each need their own fix.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Brotli2Shell, a vulnerability in Google's Brotli C decoder library, which Node.js, .NET and other software embed.

FAQ

What is Brotli2Shell?

Brotli2Shell is one of several names for CVE-2026-111497, a memory corruption flaw in Google's open-source Brotli compression library. Some researchers call it Node2Shell, after Node.js, which disclosed the flaw in its October 21 security advisory. Others use HTTP2Shell, since the same bug reaches HTTP software outside Node.js. It has circulated as Broccoli2Shell as well. We use Brotli2Shell because the bug sits in the Brotli decoder itself, not in any one downstream product.

What is the vulnerability associated with Brotli2Shell?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Google Brotli C decoder library.

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-111497

Google Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write vulnerability

9.2

An attacker can trigger the flaw by getting an application to decompress crafted Brotli data. Two common paths are a compressed HTTP response sent to a client that decompresses it automatically, and a compressed request body sent to a server that decompresses incoming content. The impact ranges from a process crash to potential remote code execution, and the bug can also leak process memory.

Note on severity scoring: Google, as the CNA, scored the flaw 9.2 (CVSSv4.0) with vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N. Microsoft rates it 8.1 (CVSSv3.1) for .NET.

When was CVE-2026-111497 first disclosed?

Google committed the upstream fix to the Brotli source repository on February 27. Node.js publicly disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 in its security advisory, the same day Google released fixed Brotli versions. Envoy Proxy and Istio had already shipped fixed releases earlier in October without naming the flaw. NVD published the CVE record on October 22. Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 both reached the Python Package Index (PyPI) on October 22. On October 25, Microsoft released .NET security updates.

What software is affected by CVE-2026-111497?

The risk applies wherever an application decompresses Brotli data an attacker can control, whether that data arrives over HTTP in either direction or inside a file.

JFrog Security Research showed that the flaw also reaches FFmpeg through the libjxl library, by way of Brotli-compressed metadata in JPEG XL files. JFrog obtained instruction-pointer control in FFmpeg with a crafted JPEG XL file but did not demonstrate code execution. The same research produced an infinite-loop denial of service in Apache Arrow, which uses Brotli for compressed Parquet data, with a crafted 534-byte input, and crashed a tested ClickHouse server with a single malformed Brotli-compressed HTTP request. Python HTTP clients such as urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp are also in scope when the Brotli or brotlicffi package is installed.

Does updating the system Brotli library fix the issue?

It depends on where the software gets its decoder. Programs that load the operating system's copy of Brotli pick up the fix once they restart. Node.js, Bun and other applications that ship with a built-in copy keep the flawed decoder until a fixed release of that application is installed.

Is every .NET, Envoy Proxy or Istio installation exposed?

No. These platforms are exposed only when Brotli decompression is in use.

.NET: Microsoft says an application "is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed," and ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are off by default. Applications are in scope when they use ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient response decompression, or the Brotli APIs in System.IO.Compression such as BrotliStream and BrotliDecoder. NativeAOT and self-contained applications pick up the fix only when they are rebuilt and redeployed. Microsoft says .NET Framework is not affected.

Envoy Proxy and Istio: Envoy Proxy is exposed only when its Brotli decompressor is configured, and Istio users are potentially affected when they enable Brotli decompression, for example through an EnvoyFilter. Istio 1.29 reached end of support on October 15. Its 1.29.9 release includes the fix.

Is PHP affected by CVE-2026-111497?

PHP's official Windows builds are affected, because they include their own copy of Brotli. On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds that bundle Brotli 1.2.1. PHP names its cURL extension as the route to the flaw in those builds, once automatic decompression of HTTP responses is enabled. cURL keeps that setting off unless an application or HTTP client library enables it. On other platforms, PHP can still reach a vulnerable decoder through the system Brotli library or through the PHP brotli extension, which bundles its own copy and fixed the flaw in version 0.21.1. The PHP source releases are unchanged, and this flaw is separate from the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities covered in our FAQ.

Is CVE-2026-111497 being exploited in the wild?

On October 26, threat intelligence firm ELLIO reported that its sensors recorded an exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-111497. ELLIO said the attempt targeted Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 and combined code copied from public PoCs with an original exploit chain. Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity. On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, with a remediation due date of November 10 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-111497 has been classified as a “Vulnerability of Interest” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available for CVE-2026-111497?

Yes. Public PoCs for CVE-2026-111497 are available on GitHub. The Imperva Red Team demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image after multiple attempts, and has not released that exploit. At least one public PoC on GitHub claims code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 under narrow lab conditions. ELLIO said it reproduced code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64.

How reliable is exploitation of CVE-2026-111497?

According to ELLIO, an exploit has to be tuned to the specific Node.js build it targets. ELLIO reported that an exploit tuned for the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64 produced nothing in 10,000 attempts against Node.js 22.23.3 and 26.12.0, which each need their own memory offsets. Even against the matching build, most of ELLIO's 400 lab attempts against an Express server crashed the worker process instead of returning a shell, but where workers restart automatically, an attacker gets repeated tries. The exploit request ELLIO captured in the wild did not produce a shell in 50 lab attempts against a vulnerable Node.js 24.22.0 target. Imperva also needed multiple attempts to achieve code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 on Linux arm64.

Are patches or mitigations available for CVE-2026-111497?

Fixed versions for Google Brotli, Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, the Python Brotli packages and PHP for Windows are listed in the table above. As of October 26, ClickHouse had merged a fix without shipping a release, and the Apache Arrow issue remained open.

Patching does not reach code that is already running. The fixed decoder takes effect in a process or scheduled job only after a restart, and in a container only after its image is rebuilt and redeployed.

Where patching is delayed, the Patch the Planet mitigation guide and the broccoli2shell.com tracker list temporary steps that reduce exposure:

Blocking requests marked Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer, so they stop before anything decompresses them. This step does nothing for applications that fetch Brotli responses from attacker-controlled servers, and turning off Brotli compression on an origin server or CDN has no effect on decompression.

Turning off Brotli decoding in HTTP clients. Taking br out of the Accept-Encoding header falls short by itself, since a hostile server can still reply with Brotli-encoded data.

Disabling the Brotli decompressor filter in Envoy Proxy and Istio in both directions. A disabled filter forwards compressed bytes as they arrive, which leaves any downstream service that decodes Brotli at risk.

Removing the Brotli or brotlicffi package from Python environments until a patched version is in place.

Are there any indicators of compromise for CVE-2026-111497?

ELLIO published the source IP address and a payload hash for the exploitation attempt it observed. They are available in ELLIO's blog post.

Has Tenable released product coverage for CVE-2026-111497?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

articles.full_text:
Learn how to use Tenable solutions to find vulnerable PHP versions, prioritize remediation, and patch the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) faster.

Key takeaways

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) put security teams in a race against attackers. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, so organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

Tenable helps you find PHP2Shell across your attack surface. Tenable One Attack Surface Management discovers externally facing PHP assets. Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center provide detections, including local checks for Linux distribution packages. Tenable One Web App Scanning assesses web applications, and Tenable One Cloud Exposure covers cloud workloads.

Tenable accelerates remediation. Tenable Patch Management matches exposures to the right patches, launches patch workflows, and validates fixes with post-scan checks. Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI lets you find vulnerable assets, create exposure initiatives, and generate remediation tickets with simple prompts.

Respond faster with Tenable solutions

The recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have put security teams in a race against attackers to remediate or mitigate exposure before their systems are targeted. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, and many of those sites run unsupported, legacy branches that no longer receive upstream support. Organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

To help cybersecurity teams accelerate emergency response, this blog outlines tips for using the Tenable solutions to identify vulnerable versions of PHP, prioritize remediation decisions, and implement patches as quickly as possible.

External Attack Surface Management

Tenable One Attack Surface Management (ASM) helps you discover externally facing assets running PHP. ASM continuously scans public data sources, such as DNS records, IP addresses, Autonomous System Numbers (ASN), WHOIS registrations, and neighboring IP ranges, to discover forgotten, rogue, or shadow IT assets that might be vulnerable to PHP2Shell. This is one of the first steps to take. It shows your digital footprint from the attacker’s perspective and identifies potential entry points into your organization.

Important ASM tips include:

Use ASM to find additional top-level domains related to your organization. Suggested Domains helps you identify additional domains you may own based on ASN, brand, domain name, IP range, subdomain, or nameserver. You can also adjust the suggestion rules to prioritize domain names based on the likelihood of ownership.

Search the inventory for PHP deployments. Create a query in ASM to identify PHP as a programming language filter. This gives you a quick starting point to assess locations, asset details, and software versions for further analysis.

Continuously monitor for changes in your attack surface. Use Subscriptions in ASM to receive event-driven notifications and understand important changes in your attack surface that may create new exposure. Choose from hundreds of pre-built event categories or create a customized subscription. Two subscriptions apply to PHP: PHP in applications and PHP end-of-life installs.

Explore the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Attack Surface Management.

How to Identify and Tag PHP Assets in Tenable One Attack Surface Management. This demo shows how to get a view of the external attack surface and identify where php2shell creates exposure. In Explore > Asset Inventory, review the inventory of assets facing the outside world. To add another inventory source, click '+' and choose an option from the drop-down menu, such as 'Add Hostnames or Domains.' In the pop-up menu, enter a new hostname, for example 'tenable.com.' To narrow the results to assets running PHP, use the query bar to set 'Programming Language' equal to 'PHP.' The results show 265 assets with PHP listed as their Programming Language. Create a 'PHP2Shell' tag and apply it to the selected assets so they can be grouped and prioritized. The Tags column then displays the 'PHP2Shell' tag. Subscriptions can be used to view and assess PHP. Subscriptions provide a growing list of events, including predefined lists and categories. Search for 'PHP' and add the 'PHP - v1' subscription. After subscribing, create an alert for the subscription. The subscription is set to 'Programming Language' contains php, so it filters assets and sends an alert when a new asset meeting this criteria is identified.

Vulnerability Management

Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center both help you find PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with detections for PHP, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions. Tenable will release additional detections as vendors publish fixes in their security advisories.

Both solutions help you create out-of-band, tactical scans based on your preferred scan policy. Additional tips include:

Update plugin feeds before running a scan. Tenable One Vulnerability Management automatically manages and updates plugin feeds through cloud synchronization by default. In offline or air-gapped environments, Tenable Security Center may require manual plugin feed updates.

Use thorough testing to discover more vulnerabilities. Enabling thorough testing and paranoia mode in your scan policy conducts deeper assessments of your attack surface using multiple methods to discover risk. This is very important when you need to scan software across all system drives or investigate deep component-level software vulnerabilities where default settings may result in false negatives.

Assign tags to indicate exposure. Use dynamic tagging to identify PHP2Shell on existing and newly discovered assets.

Actively manage open remediations. Use Exposure Response in Tenable One Vulnerability Management to create Jira tickets or ServiceNow incidents and monitor remediation progress.

Check out these solution walk-throughs to learn more about Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center:

How to Identify and Address PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities in Tenable Security Center. This demo shows how to assess and remediate disclosed PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Start the investigation by searching the complete asset inventory for potential vulnerabilities. Construct an advanced query to filter for specific known PHP-related CVEs affecting the environment. Review the IP Summary to understand the overall vulnerability posture of affected hosts with known CVEs. Use specific Tenable Plugin IDs for PHP-related vulnerabilities to uncover detailed findings across all assets. Next steps: set up a pre-configured or custom report and/or dashboard to assess the impact of PHP-related vulnerabilities across the environment.

Web App Scanning

Tenable One Web App Scanning (WAS) can help you assess your web applications for the presence of PHP2Shell, especially where PHP is embedded in content management systems (CMS), databases, and session management platforms. WAS crawls across modern web applications and APIs to identify OWASP Top 10 risks and web app component vulnerabilities. It inspects components, HTTP headers, server signatures, and cookies looking for PHP versions and associated vulnerabilities.

Tips for using WAS include:

Standard WAS scan policies will discover PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. No need to create a customized policy as long as you select all plugin groups in your scan setup. WAS assessments take longer than traditional vulnerability management scans because WAS analyzes web frameworks and responses in more depth.

Incorporate ASM results into new WAS assessments. WAS scans need known web app targets to point the scanner to assess risk. Use ASM findings to discover previously unknown web apps so that you can add them into your assessment scope.

Filter on CVEs to find results. In the Findings page, you can apply filters to see where you are exposed. Generate reports and export results to easily send to application owners and remediation teams to fix.

See the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Web App Scanning.

Patch Management

Tenable Patch Management can help you accelerate patching by matching asset and exposure findings to the patches you need to apply. You can launch patch workflows directly from Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center to define the right patch strategy based on your organization’s requirements. Tenable Patch Management enables autonomous patching, safety controls and rollbacks, and automated post-scan validation to ensure exposures have been closed.

Important Tenable Patch Management tips include:

Customize your patching strategy to address emergency vulnerabilities. Define patching schedules, deployment plans, and automation levels to address PHP2Shell and other critical out-of-band remediations.

Verify patch implementation with remediation scans. Use remediation scans to confirm patches are installed and PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are marked as fixed, or trigger an agent scan after a patch deployment finishes. You can also see the latest patch information in the plugin output.

Automatically correlate patches to vulnerable versions of PHP. Mapping patches to vulnerabilities by hand is time-consuming and error-prone. Tenable Patch Management finds the right patches for you automatically, pulling updates from official OS and third-party vendor repositories within 48 hours of release. We’ve compiled a list of vendor patches mapped to our library here.

Browse the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable Patch Management.

Cloud Security

Tenable One Cloud Exposure can help you find PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in cloud workloads using agent and agentless scanning, configuration auditing, and container inspection. Just as you would use of Tenable One Vulnerability Management, Tenable Security Center, and Tenable One Web App Scanning to address vulnerabilities in on-premises and self-managed hosts, Tenable One Cloud Exposure helps you manage and remediate vulnerabilities in Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform environments.

Tips for using Tenable One Cloud Exposure include:

Detect PHP2Shell in the Emerging Threats view. Click on the Risk tab to see the Emerging Threats page that shows all PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in one view. Toggle between virtual machines, virtual machine images, and container images to see impacted resources. This shows which resources are affected, so you can triage issues and accelerate remediation workflows.

Create a policy to detect and respond to PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Create a response playbook based on you business rules and preferences. Custom policies enable you to define rules, schedule reports, and create step-by-step remediation guides to fix issues immediately.

Leverage integrated remediation workflows. For Infrastructure as Code (IaC) environments, use auto-generated IaC snippets supporting Terraform, CloudFormation, and JSON to push code-level corrections straight to your repositories. Otherwise, you can route service tickets into your existing IT and DevOps workflows to automate processes.

View the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Cloud Exposure.

How to address PHP2Shell in Tenable One Cloud Exposure. This demo covers using Hexa, the PHP2Shell Emerging Threats dashboard, Explorer queries, custom policies, custom dashboards, scheduled reports, and risk automations to identify, track, and remediate PHP2Shell exposures. Orientation with Hexa: Ask Hexa orientation questions such as "how can PHP2Shell be exploited in my infrastructure?" Hexa returns a summary of what PHP2Shell does, how an attacker might attempt to exploit it, and recommended next steps for exposures found in the environment. Exploitation paths vary. PHP2Shell Dashboard: Navigate to Risk in the left navigation, then Emerging Threats, then PHP2Shell. The dashboard gives an end-to-end view of resources affected by PHP2Shell. Filter by infrastructure type, such as Container Images, Virtual Machines, and Virtual Machine Images. Use filters and Group By options to organize the data to fit how a team operates. To drill down, click the Vulnerability column for the first affected container image under the Container Registry account. Its properties can be reviewed to prioritize remediation and close exposures before exploitation. Under the Overview tab, the Plugins section lists Plugin ID 369483, which contains CVE-2026-109618. Clicking the plugin ID shows plugin details for the container image carrying the critical PHP2Shell CVE, along with remediation instructions. Remediation through Cloud Findings: Click the affected container image, open the Cloud Findings tab, and select a finding. Open the Remediation tab for instructions on remediating the container image. Instructions vary by finding; in this example the operating system needs to be updated. Explorer queries: Go to Explore in the left navigation, then Explorer. A custom query finds two CVEs related to PHP2Shell. Clicking a resource shows an overview, cloud findings, threat detections, vulnerabilities, and more. Save the query with the button in the upper right to turn on tracking for later use, additional dashboards, and reporting. The saved query is named "PHP2Shell - tracking." Complex queries: Queries can find different forms of Toxic Combinations or identify old VMs and images, which can prompt shutting down or isolating old systems. The example query asks which systems with PHP2Shell share the same toxic combination as "X public workloads" with critical vulnerabilities and high privileges. Custom policy: A custom policy simplifies administration of PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It lets a team ignore or close individual instances, add automations, notes, time boundaries, and more. Navigate to Policies, then Cloud Policies, select Custom, and click Create Custom Policy. Select Query, choose the saved query "PHP2Shell - tracking," and click Create in the bottom right. Custom dashboard: To show PHP2Shell data on login to Tenable One Cloud Exposure, go to Dashboards, then All Dashboards, then click Create Dashboard. Select the saved query "PHP2Shell - tracking," drag and drop widgets onto the dashboard, and click Save for a quick snapshot on opening Tenable One Cloud Exposure. Recurring daily report: In Explorer, select the "PHP2Shell - tracking" query, click Add in the right corner, and select Report. Schedule a daily PHP2Shell report to be sent, in this example through Microsoft Teams to members of the General channel every morning. Automation for new findings: To trigger notifications when new PHP2Shell resources appear, create an automated workflow based on the saved query. Navigate to Operations in the main navigation, then Risk Automations, then Create Automation. Select the PHP2Shell tracker query from the drop-down and click Create in the bottom right.

Exposure Management with Tenable Hexa AI

Tenable One includes all of the capabilities mentioned above and more. One important capability that’s only available in Tenable One is Tenable Hexa AI, the agentic AI engine that can answer questions, automate tasks, execute workflows, and more. Tenable Hexa AI can speed up your response to critical vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell.

Key Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI tips include:

Find all PHP2Shell vulnerable assets and PHP installations. Simply click on Tenable Hexa AI and type “find all open vulnerabilities for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619” or “find all instances of PHP and create a new tag based on version number,” and Tenable Hexa AI will complete the request in minutes.

Create new remediation initiatives and track status. Prompting Tenable Hexa AI to “create an exposure initiative for PHP2Shell,” will automatically define the initiative, create SLAs and provide the description and vulnerability filters. You can see the latest status of your PHP2Shell initiative in Exposure Response to help communicate progress to stakeholders.

Automatically generate remediation tickets to address PHP2Shell. Use Tenable Hexa AI to create remediation tickets with a simple prompt such as “create remediation tickets for all systems vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Assign the severity level as Critical and the due date as Immediate.”

Explore the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI.

How to Identify, Prioritize, and Remediate php2shell Using Tenable One Exposure Management and Tenable Hexa AI. The demo starts by identifying overall exposure to php2shell. In Hexa AI, a prompt asks Hexa to find all php2shell vulnerability findings. Hexa finds 2,007 instances and provides an overview of the top 15. From there, all findings can be explored in the Exposure Findings view, which lists the full set of findings sorted by asset exposure score (AES). AES provides a way to prioritize the most important remediation actions. Next, remediation progress is tracked by returning to Hexa and prompting it to create an exposure initiative. The resulting initiative page is opened with the view option. On this page, tickets can be assigned and remediation status can be tracked for all php2shell vulnerabilities. Instead of creating tickets manually, Hexa can create them. Ticketing instructions are provided to Hexa, which asks the user to confirm the ticketing software to use. Jira is selected. Submitting the request automatically creates tickets on the user's behalf. A link is provided to learn more about Hexa AI.

Want to learn more?
