articles.title: The adversary economy: How threat actors are reacting to PHP2Shell
articles.context: They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation,...
articles.full_text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities sent criminal forum operators scrambling to protect their own infrastructure, revealing that threat actors face the same exposure management challenges as the organizations they target.

Key takeaways

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy.

Forum self-evacuations: Criminal forums including BreachForums initiated emergency infrastructure migrations, taking themselves offline within hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, citing direct risk to their operations.

Underground operators face a dual threat: both law enforcement and rival criminal groups could weaponize PHP2Shell against forum infrastructure storing member identities, private communications, and stolen credentials.

The adversary response mirrors legitimate enterprise incident response, including emergency patching, platform migration, and business continuity planning.

Historical precedent from the 2024 BreachForums seizure conditioned criminal operators to treat infrastructure vulnerabilities as existential business risks

Background

PHP powers an estimated 75% of websites with identifiable server-side technology, making it the backbone of the modern web. That infrastructure extends far beyond legitimate businesses. Criminal forums, dark web marketplaces, and underground communication platforms rely on the same PHP-based software stacks, such as phpBB, custom forum engines, and web-based administration panels, that power their legitimate counterparts.

On Oct. 20, 2026, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP were publicly disclosed: CVE-2026-109618 (OOM Corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (Stale Global State), each carrying a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. The two flaws target different stages of PHP’s memory management, and chaining them together yields a more reliable exploitation path than either alone. Researchers credit frontier AI models with both the initial discovery and the exploitation chain connecting them. Tenable Vulnerability Watch classified both as Vulnerabilities of Concern (VOC). Within hours, the cybersecurity community began its familiar cycle of assessment, patching, and remediation. (For a full technical breakdown, see our blog “php2shell: Frequently asked questions about critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities”.)

At the same time, a parallel response was already underway including criminal forum self-evacuations and steps to protect the adversary economy.

“We take our security seriously”

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy. Criminal operators invest in infrastructure, manage risk, plan for business continuity, and respond to threats against their operations with the same systematic urgency that any well-run organization would apply. From the credential theft supply chains we documented earlier this year to the infrastructure-level emergency playing out now, a consistent pattern emerges: the underground functions as an economy, and economies have attack surfaces. PHP2Shell affected both sides of the security divide simultaneously, and the underground's response demonstrates that sophisticated threat actors have already internalized the severity of this exposure.

Within 48 hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, administrators across multiple major criminal forums posted emergency notices to their communities. BreachForums, one of the largest English-language criminal marketplaces, posted an advisory that included a phrase familiar to anyone who has read a corporate breach notification: “We take our security seriously.”

The irony is difficult to overstate. A platform best known for trafficking stolen credentials, facilitating ransomware operations, and hosting leaked corporate data deployed the same language that Fortune 500 companies use after their own security incidents. But behind the borrowed corporate-speak was genuine operational urgency.

BreachForums was not alone. DarkForums posted its own shutdown notice: “DF will remain offline until PHP has been patched globally.” PwnForums went dark without explanation. Dread, the Reddit-like platform serving the Tor ecosystem, posted a maintenance notice explicitly naming both CVEs. Several forums temporarily restricted new registrations, and others migrated critical communications to Telegram channels as a contingency measure, treating their PHP-based web platforms as potentially compromised infrastructure.

The dual threat

The urgency behind these evacuations reflects a threat model that legitimate organizations would recognize immediately. Criminal forums run on PHP infrastructure, and that infrastructure stores exactly the kind of data that makes a vulnerability like PHP2Shell catastrophic.

The simultaneous self-evacuation is a significant behavioral indicator. Analysis from DarkOwl, a dark web intelligence firm, highlighted the scope of what sits behind a typical forum’s PHP application layer: member email addresses, IP logs, private messages, financial transaction records, and the very stolen credentials that members uploaded for sale. A successful exploit of a forum’s PHP stack would not merely disrupt the platform. It would expose the identities and operational security of every participant.

Forum operators face a threat that most legitimate businesses do not: the adversary attacks from two directions simultaneously. Law enforcement agencies have demonstrated both the capability and the willingness to exploit criminal infrastructure, as the FBI’s operation against Hive ransomware and multiple forum takedowns have shown. But rival criminal groups represent an equally serious threat. Competing forums, extortionists, and opportunistic hackers all have incentive to breach a rival platform’s database to steal its user base, to extort its operators, or to eliminate competition.

This dual threat transforms a PHP vulnerability from a technical issue into an existential business risk. The criminal underground last evacuated platforms at this scale during the 2024 BreachForums seizure — but that response was triggered by law enforcement action. PHP2Shell marks the first time a technical vulnerability in shared infrastructure provoked the same reaction, a shift suggesting criminal operators now treat their PHP dependency as a systemic single point of failure. They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation, but when.

The BreachForums lesson

That institutional memory was shaped by hard experience. The 2024 FBI seizure of BreachForums demonstrated in concrete terms what happens when criminal infrastructure is compromised.

That seizure resulted in the exposure of operational details, the arrest of the forum’s administrator, and the disruption of thousands of active criminal operations that depended on the platform. For the underground economy, it was the equivalent of a major supply chain breach: a single point of failure that cascaded across an entire ecosystem.

The lesson was absorbed. Criminal operators began treating their web infrastructure as a single point of failure requiring the same resilience planning that legitimate enterprises apply to critical systems. PHP2Shell validated that concern. The two CVEs affect every PHP version below 8.3, meaning that the approximately 59% of internet-facing PHP hosts running end-of-life branches are permanently exposed absent a version upgrade. Criminal forums running older PHP versions face the same impossible math as any enterprise with a large install base of unsupported software: the patch does not exist, and the only remediation is migration.

From defense to offense: the exploit economy

The criminal underground’s relationship with PHP2Shell extends beyond defensive measures. Intelligence reporting indicates that exploit code for both CVEs circulated in private channels before the public embargo lifted, with pre-disclosure exploitation observed as early as Oct. 17 from infrastructure traced to an IP address geolocated in Australia.

The exploit development pipeline has accelerated in ways that should concern every organization running PHP. Researchers have documented the use of AI-assisted vulnerability analysis tools to accelerate the development of working exploits and to identify additional exploitation vectors within the disclosed vulnerability classes. This represents a broader trend in which the same AI capabilities that accelerate defensive security research simultaneously compress the window between disclosure and weaponization.

The monetization forecast follows a pattern we have documented before. The developer credential economy operates through three layers (generation, distribution, and weaponization), and PHP2Shell maps cleanly onto each. Initial access brokers will package PHP2Shell exploitation into their service offerings. Ransomware affiliates will incorporate the vulnerabilities into their initial access playbooks. And the criminal forums that patched their own infrastructure will become the marketplaces for selling access to organizations that did not. We saw a preview of this commoditization cycle during the Miasma campaign, where open-sourced attack toolchains accelerated exploitation at scale. The adversary economy is efficient: the same operators who scrambled to protect their own PHP stacks will profit from organizations that fail to do the same.

What this means for defenders

The criminal underground’s reaction to PHP2Shell is, paradoxically, one of the clearest available signals of the vulnerability’s severity. When threat actors treat a disclosure as an emergency requiring immediate operational response, defenders should calibrate their own urgency accordingly.

Organizations running PHP should treat both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as immediate remediation priorities. Every PHP version below 8.3 is affected, and no patches will be issued for end-of-life branches including all of PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, 8.1, and 8.2. For environments where an immediate upgrade is not feasible, compensating controls including web application firewalls, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for exploitation indicators should be deployed without delay. The criminals have already patched. The question for every organization is whether they will do the same before the exploit economy catches up.

Identifying affected systems

A list of Tenable plugins for these vulnerabilities can be found on the individual CVE pages for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as they’re released. This link will display all available plugins for these vulnerabilities, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

articles.title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
articles.context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
articles.full_text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Check back next week when we’ll finish our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series with a blog about the cybersecurity challenges of state and local governments. Read the first two blogs in the series:

How to mitigate the risk from AI-generated apps built by your '‘citizen coder’ employees

Critical infrastructure orgs face heightened cyber risk from nation-state groups, AI threats

To learn more about shadow AI and how Tenable can help you address this issue, check out the following resources:

articles.title: How Tenable brought multi-language support to security detectors with agentic translation
articles.context: AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection
articles.full_text:
AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection. Here’s how Tenable trained our threat detectors to process nine additional languages and understand thousands more, without the need for a translation model, which increases costs and slows down processing.

Key takeaways

Tenable One AI Exposure’s detectors, covering AI threats, harmful content, and other policy risks, were originally English-centric. To assess threats written in other languages, our product translated them into English, a slow, expensive, and often imprecise approach.

Tenable built an agentic translation pipeline that generates high-fidelity, label-preserving training and benchmark data across nine languages, guarded by a multi-judge quality gate, a refinement loop, and a model-refusal handling fallback.

This single multilingual model detects threats natively in all 10 supported languages. Compared with our previous process of translating threats into English, this model is roughly 20-800 times faster per item and is less expensive by an order of magnitude, bearing a one-time cost that does not grow with usage traffic from our customers.

Why your AI security tool should support multiple languages

A prompt attack against an AI model written in Spanish, Arabic, or Hindi is every bit as dangerous as one written in English, which is why an English-only AI security detector will leave your organization at risk from non-English attacks.

To address this issue in our product, Tenable first adopted a “translate-then-detect” process:

Identify the language.

Translate the input to English with a large translation model.

Then run the English detector.

This process works, but it has four downsides:

Latency. A large, autoregressive translation model that runs before every non-English detection needs hundreds of milliseconds for short inputs, and seconds to tens of seconds for long ones.

Cost. Every non-English request pays for a full translation pass.

Operational overhead. You have to serve, scale, and maintain another heavyweight model.

Lost signal. Meaning and intent blur in naive translation, which degrades the tool’s ability to detect threats.

How Tenable turned our AI security tool into a polyglot

To make our AI security product natively multilingual, we discovered that we didn’t need to use a translator LLM in production. Instead, we found that we needed high-quality multilingual data in two places:

A training set to teach the model the target languages.

A test set we could trust to benchmark performance honestly in each language.

Both must preserve the labels of the data, ensuring that the label survives the translation process. Translation can quietly flip a label (a malicious data sample rendered as a benign one) or defang it (the security-relevant language “bite” softened so that what’s a clear positive in the original language instead reads as a borderline threat). Either way, the data sample is now mislabeled and poisons the data.

Tenable concluded that the following methods are not ideal:

Human-expert translation. It is slow and needs a fluent reviewer for every language, so it does not scale.

Machine translation. Standard translation methods distort dataset quality in two distinct ways: native machine translation prioritizes smooth phrasing over security context, potentially stripping out malicious intent (e.g., turning a toxin synthesis request into a benign chemistry query), while direct, word-for-word translation creates awkward, unnaturally phrased text that degrades training signal, such as an English phishing lure translated literally into Japanese.

Off-the-shelf LLMs. They may refuse to translate material they flag as inappropriate, such as prompts about weapons synthesis or self-harm topics, so the text that represents a likely threat gets left out of the dataset.

Always-on (online) translators. Relying on online translation pipelines introduces per-request latency, operational complexity, and costs that scale with hundreds of millions of items, making it impractical for production environments.

The translation process has to be cost-effective and repeatable across many languages.

The Tenable solution: An agentic pipeline plus a multilingual model

1. The agentic pipeline overview

The agentic translation pipeline. Each English item is transcreated by a frontier LLM, scored by a panel of independent judges, and either accepted or sent back to refine. On a refusal, a controlled open-source model takes over, via the same gate.

In Tenable’s data translation process, every item flows through three stages in our agentic pipeline.

Translate. A frontier LLM produces a transcreation, a translation that we fine-tune by specifying the task, the item’s label, and the target language, as opposed to a blind word-for-word rendering. This fine-tuning is precisely what keeps the security-relevant meaning, and the label, intact.

Estimate. A panel of independent judges scores each translation for fluency, meaning integrity, and whether the original data label still holds.

Gate. Only translations that clear every check are kept.

Two recovery loops keep the hard cases from being lost:

Refusal handling. When the frontier translator refuses a sensitive item, the pipeline hands the same transcreation job to a controlled, open-source small-language model that does not refuse, and its output goes through the same quality gate, so legitimate-but-sensitive security data is not silently dropped.

Refinement. When a translation fails the quality gate, it is sent back for another attempt rather than thrown away.

Because the task and labels are parameters, the pipeline can serve any future detection task requiring multilingual support.

2. A pretrained multilingual model

Instead of training a language model from scratch, we fine-tuned a compact model that was already pretrained on many languages, which yielded two benefits:

It consumes far less data per language. The model has already learned useful cross-lingual representations, so we only taught it our task.

It transfers knowledge between languages. We measured this before spending a dollar on translation. For some tasks, the model successfully generalized to other languages using only English training data, eliminating the need for translation. For harder tasks, we used the agentic translation framework to translate only to the languages in which the model underperformed. Even in those cases, training the model on a handful of languages lifted the model’s translation performance in other languages at no additional cost.

Impact and results

By replacing our legacy translate-then-detect architecture with a single native model, Tenable transformed our pipeline into an enterprise-grade solution that delivers near-instantaneous global coverage. This shift drastically reduced latency and infrastructure costs while maintaining top-tier quality and unlocking broader language support. Below are the key results achieved by this upgraded architecture:

One fast model, no translator in the path. Detection now runs natively in every supported language in tens of milliseconds, whereas it took seconds with the translate-then-detect process, roughly 20-800× faster per item. In addition, the memory footprint is about 12-14× smaller: under 1 GB versus 12-14 GB.

A one-time cost, under $10,000. We generated the multilingual training and benchmark data once. That cost does not grow with client’s production traffic, unlike an always-on translator, whose bill scales with every request.

Budget-tunable by design. We set the budget, and the pipeline adjusts the tier of LLM it uses and how much refinement each item receives.

Quality you can prove. A neutral LLM-as-a-judge from a third-party model family, outside our translation and grading stack, preferred Tenable transcreations over those from a commercial machine translation model and over those from a strong open translation model in the large majority of head-to-head comparisons.

No English regression. Every Tenable One AI Exposure detector gained the ability to understand and translate from nine languages (Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, and Hindi) while English performance held or improved, and latency stayed near real-time.

Reach beyond the languages we trained. Because the model was pretrained on a very broad set of languages, the same model can read and flag attacks in thousands of languages we never explicitly trained it on. We have only formally validated the 10 languages we support, so this wider reach is promising but needs further testing before it can be relied on.

AI-threat detection, recall @ 0.005% false positive rate. (The recall metric measures how good a system is at finding every single relevant item without missing any.) Our multilingual model matches or beats translate-then-detect on 9 of 10 languages and overall (0.93 vs 0.88).

Harmful-content detection, recall @ 0.02% false positive rate. On the harder task, the gap widens: our multilingual model leads on every language and overall (0.65 vs 0.50).

How Tenable One AI Exposure protects multilingual users

Threat actors do not limit themselves to English, and neither should your defenses. With this work, Tenable One AI Exposure extends the same detection quality (for jailbreaks, prompt injection, harmful content, and data exposure) natively across 10 languages, at production speed and without a translation bottleneck in the request path. As customers adopt AI in more markets and more languages, that multilingual coverage extends with them.

Learn more about Tenable One AI Exposure

articles.context: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Patches are available for supported PHP 8.x branches, and exploitation attempts began before public disclosure.
articles.full_text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Patches are available for supported PHP 8.x branches, and exploitation attempts began before public disclosure.

Change log

Update October 28: Clarified Amazon Threat Intelligence's wording to say php2shell is seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Added Dream Research's report of a campaign that chained php2shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) to gain root access on firewalls.

Click here to review the change log history

Update October 28: Clarified Amazon Threat Intelligence's wording to say php2shell is seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Added Dream Research's report of a campaign that chained php2shell with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) to gain root access on firewalls.

Update October 26: CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its KEV catalog. Added details on a regression in PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 and on PHP's October 23 session upload progress advisory. Added a note on restarting PHP services after updating. Added Adel Karimi's report of successful exploitation against honeypot servers and Trail of Bits' report of working exploits against pre-patch PHP releases. Linked our Brotli2Shell FAQ for a separate fix in PHP's Windows builds.

Update October 23: Updated the Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security patch to SC-202610.2 and added a Tenable knowledge base article.

Update October 23: Added guidance on authenticated scanning and a dedicated view in Tenable Cloud Security. Reorganized the Tenable product coverage section.

Update October 23: Updated the example Tenable Hexa AI prompt.

Update October 22: Added security patch SC-202610.1 for Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security, plus a CyberAgents Exchange skill for reporting php2shell exposure. Added the status of these vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog along with CISA's October 21 alert.

Update October 21: Added Amazon Threat Intelligence's report of exploitation attempts beginning October 17, before public disclosure. Added Tenable Nessus plugins, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions, along with guidance on using Tenable Hexa AI to find vulnerable PHP installations and create remediation tickets.

Update October 21: PHP released patches and published its advisories. This post now includes vulnerability details, fixed versions, source backports for end-of-life branches, interim mitigation guidance, updated exploitation details and Tenable product coverage and Vulnerability Watch classification.

October 21: Original publication based on limited public information ahead of PHP's official advisory.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The PHP security team rates both CVSSv4.0 9.2 and says they can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Amazon Threat Intelligence observed an exploitation attempt on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It says php2shell "is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild." On October 26, CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

On October 21, 2026, PHP released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. End-of-life branches will not receive official releases, but the PHP security team published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4 through 8.1.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that were announced on October 20, 2026.

FAQ

When were these PHP vulnerabilities first disclosed?

On October 20, 2026, the CVE identifiers circulated on Hacker News and social media. Later that day, the PHP security team published an advance notice of a security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM ET) to address two critical vulnerabilities. The notice said the team could release earlier if details became public or if exploitation appeared in the wild. CERT-EU also published an advisory (2026-018) naming both CVEs. According to the PHP Foundation, the release was originally scheduled for October 22 and was moved up by a day after the CVE identifiers leaked. On October 21, the PHP security team published its security advisory and released patches.

A video shared by researcher Kirill Firsov demonstrates the exploit chain, dubbed php2shell. Firsov credited the video and exploit to researcher LCFR of Calif.io, which has since published a technical writeup. The PHP Foundation credited Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, among others, for their research and responsible disclosure. Calif and Wiz have both said they used AI models in their research.

The PHP security team is giving advance notice: Upcoming security release Wed, Oct 21st 2026, 14:00UTC, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSSv4 9.2.PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update. Earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence.

— The PHP Foundation (@ThePHPF) October 20, 2026

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-109618

PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (OOM Corruption)

9.2

CVE-2026-109619

PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (Stale Global State)

9.2

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 stems from how PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) errors. If memory runs out while PHP's internal request data is only partially initialized, the cleanup that follows can treat that data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw. Leftover state from one request points to freed memory, and a later request handled by the same worker can then use it. According to PHP, both can be exploited by an unauthenticated remote attacker. PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 also lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact.

PHP says every installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit can be triggered by an unauthenticated request before any application code runs.

CVSS scores differ across sources. The PHP security team rates both vulnerabilities as CVSSv4.0 9.2. According to the PHP Foundation, the CVE identifiers that circulated before the release came with an incorrect CVSS score of 10.0.

Which PHP versions are affected?

According to Calif's technical writeup, the earliest affected code path it found dates to PHP 5.4.0. The PHP security team released the following fixed versions:

Fixed Version

8.2.35

PHP 7.4.x through 8.1.x

No official release; minimal source backports from the PHP security team

PHP 5.4.x through 7.3.x

End-of-life, no fix from the PHP project

According to PHP, Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance. If you use distribution packages, check your vendor's advisories.

On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds, 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, that fix a separate vulnerability in their bundled Brotli library, CVE-2026-111497. The PHP source and runtime versions are unchanged. For details, see our Brotli2Shell FAQ.

How widespread is PHP, and how many hosts are potentially affected?

According to W3Techs, PHP is used by 69.3% of websites whose server-side language is known. Platforms such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Laravel and Magento all run on PHP. Calif says it confirmed pre-authentication remote code execution against specific versions of popular PHP applications, including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento. Security researcher Silas Cutler's rough estimate is that over 1.3 million internet-exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable. A Shodan search by Henk Poley counts over 1.9 million internet-exposed hosts running PHP.

Has exploitation been observed in the wild?

On October 21, Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said the company is "seeing early attacks emerging" and is updating its mitigations as new attack vectors appear. watchTowr says it has reproduced both vulnerabilities and is observing exploitation attempts against both.

Amazon Threat Intelligence said it observed a php2shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It said it is unclear how the attacker obtained exploit information. More attempts followed on October 21, with payloads and infrastructure that Amazon says suggest multiple actors. Amazon says it is unclear whether any of the October 21 attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems. It also says php2shell "is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild." It recommends starting investigations from at least October 17, not from the disclosure date.

On October 24, security researcher Adel Karimi reported successful exploitation against three honeypot servers running PHP 8.4.26. The exploit requests started shells that ran attacker commands. The report says the activity is consistent with CVE-2026-109618, and that it does not show use of CVE-2026-109619. It also says the traffic closely matches a family of publicly available proof-of-concept exploits. The honeypots used a single-worker Apache mod_php setup that was intentionally favorable to the exploit, and the report says the results are not a measure of how reliably the exploit works on other setups.

On October 26, Dream Research reported finding artifacts of a campaign that chained a custom php2shell exploit with CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw known as Fragnesia that we covered in a separate FAQ. According to Dream, the attacker gained root access on 24 internet-facing firewalls from an unnamed vendor, then used the same chain on an internal firewall management server reached through one of them. Some of these systems "appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment." Dream said the php2shell exploit was not a public one and needed precise memory offsets for each version of the firewall software. Dream has not named the vendor or the affected versions, and Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity.

PHP sites behind Cloudflare already have an initial set of WAF rules deployed for the known exploit vectors in these vulnerabilities. The rules are available to all customers, including free.We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up.This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as @ThePHPF releases the update at 14:00 UTC today.

— Dane Knecht 🦭 (@dok2001) October 21, 2026

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Code claiming to exploit these vulnerabilities is circulating publicly, but we have not verified that any of it works against CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. Unverified exploit code is sometimes laced with malware, so treat it with caution. The PHP Foundation said the PHP security team inspected PoCs that appeared after the leak but "did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure."

Since then, on October 26, Trail of Bits said it confirmed that php2shell exploits work against pre-patch releases of PHP 8.2 through 8.5, and its demo showed a shell on MediaWiki, Symfony, Laravel and phpBB.

Are patches or mitigations available?

Yes. The PHP security team released fixed versions on October 21 (see the table above). For end-of-life branches, it published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4 through 8.1, for those who build from source. If you run another end-of-life version, upgrade to a supported release or ask your distribution or LTS vendor.

The PHP security team says updating is the only complete fix. For organizations that cannot update immediately, PHP's advisory lists configuration changes that reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe. For CVE-2026-109618, PHP lists setting memory_limit=-1 in a way applications cannot override. For CVE-2026-109619, it lists setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. PHP says to restart every PHP worker after these changes. PHP also suggests a container or cgroup memory limit as an availability boundary, though it says this is not a complete mitigation either.

Installing updated PHP packages does not patch PHP processes that are already running. Google Cloud's guidance, which includes input from Mandiant, notes that PHP-FPM, Apache and other services that run PHP keep the vulnerable code in memory until they are restarted. The same guidance says to capture worker memory from servers that show signs of probing before restarting them, because a restart erases that evidence.

CERT-EU also recommends that organizations that cannot update right away consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is applied and verified.

Cloudflare has deployed WAF rules for the known exploit vectors, available to all customers including the free tier. Cloudflare describes this as a stopgap only. The rules only cover traffic routed through Cloudflare.

Are there known issues with the new PHP releases?

PHP developers confirmed a regression in PHP 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 that can crash PHP processes in some applications that use the SimpleXML extension. It is tracked as php-src issue #24488. PHP developers traced it to a separate garbage collector fix included in those releases, not to the patches for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619. A fix has been merged into the PHP source but, as of October 26, has not shipped in a release.

On October 23, PHP published an informational advisory about what it calls an unlikely remote code execution vector in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. PHP says it only occurs under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. Until its next regular bugfix release, PHP suggests setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0, the same setting its CVE-2026-109619 advisory listed as a mitigation.

Have PHP vulnerabilities been exploited before?

Yes. Before php2shell, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog included three vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Two of them are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns:

Have these vulnerabilities been added to the CISA KEV catalog?

Yes. On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to the KEV catalog, with a remediation due date of October 29 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified these vulnerabilities as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been classified as “Vulnerability of Concern” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is Tenable affected by these vulnerabilities?

Tenable Security Center and Tenable Enclave Security include PHP. Out of caution, Tenable released stand-alone security patch SC-202610.2 for both products on October 23. It updates PHP to 8.2.35. Details are available in TNS-2026-30 for Tenable Security Center and TNS-2026-31 for Tenable Enclave Security. Tenable customers can find patch release notes in this knowledge base article. Advisories for Tenable products are published at tenable.com/security.

Do scans need to be authenticated?

For PHP installed on hosts, credentialed or agent scans give the most complete results. Tenable Nessus plugin 369483 uses both local and remote checks. An unauthenticated scan can detect a vulnerable version only if the host exposes its PHP version over the network, so results vary by host. For web applications, Tenable One Web App Scanning plugins 115719 to 115722 work without authentication and check the PHP version the application exposes.

How can Tenable customers find affected assets?

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can use the Software tab in Explore to find assets running PHP. Filter by Product is equal to PHP, then compare each asset's PHP version against the fixed versions above. The tab is populated from scan results, so run credentialed or agent scans regularly to keep it current.

Customers can also use Tenable One Attack Surface Management to find public-facing assets running PHP with this query: Programming Languages contains PHP.

Microsoft patched 1,407 CVEs in its October 2026 Patch Tuesday release, with 69 rated critical, 1,337 rated as important, and one rated as low.

Elevation of Privilege (EoP) vulnerabilities accounted for 47.9% of the vulnerabilities patched this month, followed by remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities at 22.3%.

Important

CVE-2026-96951 | Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability

CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass vulnerability affecting Windows Shell. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and was rated as important. According to Microsoft, this vulnerability was exploited in the wild as a zero-day.

An attacker could exploit this vulnerability using social engineering tactics, via email or messages, to convince their target to open a malicious file. Successful exploitation would bypass the Mark of the Web (MOTW) security feature.

This is the third flaw in Windows Shell that was exploited in the wild in 2026: CVE-2026-21510 was patched in February 2026’s Patch Tuesday while CVE-2026-32202 was patched in April 2026’s Patch Tuesday.

Important

CVE-2026-108398 |.NET Framework security feature bypass vulnerability

CVE-2026-108398 is a security feature bypass vulnerability affecting.NET Framework. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as important. It was publicly disclosed prior to a patch being available.

An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by registering a malicious.NET assembly on a vulnerable system to be loaded by a protected process. Successful exploitation would allow the attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC).

Critical

CVE-2026-70229 | Windows Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-70229 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.1 and is rated as critical. Microsoft assesses this vulnerability as “Exploitation More Likely” according to Microsoft’s Exploitability Index.

An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted packet to the vulnerable AD DS service. Successful exploitation could grant an attacker code execution on the vulnerable system.

Important

CVE-2026-70279 | Microsoft Exchange Server spoofing vulnerability

CVE-2026-70279 is a spoofing vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 9.3 and is rated as important. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.” An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a target through social engineering to click on a malicious link. Successful exploitation against a target with administrative privileges would allow an attacker to access or modify organizational data.

Critical

CVE-2026-70571 | Microsoft Exchange Server remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-70571 is a remote code execution vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.1 and is rated as critical. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a malicious email to a vulnerable Microsoft Exchange server that would cause it to process the email using internal content-conversion. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker the ability to execute code on the Exchange server.
